\section{Results}\label{sec:results}
Unless noted, results are averages over the 41 decontaminated tasks and five seeds.

\paragraph{Noise floors.} Table~\ref{tab:ceil} lists the estimates. $\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{floor}}$ ranges from 0.31 to 0.92 pChEMBL units and $R^2_{\max}$ from 0.30 to 0.96. The median $\hat s$ is 0.54 for $K_i$ tasks and 0.55 for $\mathrm{IC}_{50}$ tasks, of the same order as earlier ChEMBL-wide estimates for $K_i$ (0.54)~\cite{kramer2012experimental} and the reported 25\% larger spread of $\mathrm{IC}_{50}$ data~\cite{kalliokoski2013comparability}; in our set the measurement type is confounded with target class ($K_i$ tasks are mostly GPCRs, $\mathrm{IC}_{50}$ tasks mostly kinases), so we do not attribute the difference to the measurement type. Replicates are often concentrated in few document pairs: CHEMBL237\_IC50 rests on 7 document pairs, one of which contributes 79\% of molecule pairs. Accordingly, the bootstrap over document pairs gives intervals more than 20\% wider than the bootstrap over molecules for 30 of 41 tasks, and up to 6 times as wide for the two extremes, CHEMBL5113\_Ki and CHEMBL2971\_IC50 (for the latter, 0.53--1.15); it is narrower only for tasks with many document pairs. Table~\ref{tab:robust} shows the sensitivity to curation: counting identical values from different documents once raises $\hat s$ by up to 0.20 (CHEMBL4040\_IC50), and a stereo-aware molecule definition changes it by more than 0.05 for 17 tasks. These are the uncertainties of the reference point against which all models below are scored.

\paragraph{Fraction of ceiling.} Table~\ref{tab:frac} gives mean $f$ by model and split. ECFP+RF is the best model on every split. On random splits its mean $f$ is 1.04, but the median is 0.93, the mean without the tasks where it exceeds 1 is 0.83, and computing the floor at the ends of the confidence interval of $\hat s$ moves the mean between 0.89 and 1.33. On scaffold and temporal splits the means are 0.87 and 0.42 (medians 0.74 and 0.35), and 0.38 on the document-grouped split of Section~\ref{sec:docsplit}. The apparent ease of random splits is not a property of the chemistry: Section~\ref{sec:support} shows that it comes from training molecules drawn from the test molecule's own source document, and once documents are kept apart the best model reaches about 38\% of the ceiling rather than passing it.

\paragraph{ECFP versus frozen embeddings.} Frozen ChemBERTa-77M and MoLFormer-XL-10\% embeddings with a GBM head are below ECFP+GBM on every split (Table~\ref{tab:paired}, Figure~\ref{fig:paired}): by 0.19--0.25 in $f$ on random and scaffold splits, where they are worse on all 41 tasks, and by 0.07--0.08 on temporal splits, where they are better on only 9--12 of 41 tasks (Holm-adjusted $p\le0.002$ in all cases). ECFP+RF is slightly better than ECFP+GBM (0.02--0.04 in $f$; better on 30--32 of 41 tasks). In a three-task pilot (CHEMBL237\_IC50, CHEMBL206\_IC50, CHEMBL204\_Ki) frozen embeddings had appeared better than ECFP on temporal splits; on 41 tasks this did not hold. The conclusion concerns two small frozen models with a tree-based head, not pretrained models in general.

\paragraph{D-MPNN and fine-tuning.} Table~\ref{tab:subset} compares all models on the 5 tasks where the D-MPNN and fine-tuned ChemBERTa were run. On random and scaffold splits neither reaches ECFP, and fine-tuning does not improve on the frozen embedding. On temporal splits the fine-tuned model has the highest mean (0.31 versus 0.28 for ECFP+RF), but this comes from a single task, CHEMBL237\_IC50 (0.48 versus 0.08); on the other 4 tasks the fine-tuned model averages 0.27 against 0.33 for ECFP+RF. With 5 tasks we do not test these differences.

\paragraph{Models below the noise floor.} On 25 task--split combinations ECFP+RF scores $f>1$, i.e.\ its test RMSE is below the estimated floor (Figure~\ref{fig:floor}), 17 of them on random splits and none on the document-grouped split. If between-document noise were independent of what a model can learn, this would be impossible in expectation~\cite{kolmar2021noise}; models reaching or exceeding noise-based bounds were also reported by Crusius et al.~\cite{crusius2025fitting}. Section~\ref{sec:support} shows that these cases are not scattered anomalies: $f$ rises with the estimated noise it is meant to divide out, and what carries a model past the floor is how many training molecules come from the test molecule's own source document. Models are known to exploit publication-level signals in ChEMBL~\cite{blevins2025cleverhans}. Floor mis-estimation contributes as well for individual tasks --- for CHEMBL2971\_IC50 the interval over document pairs is very wide (0.53--1.15), and two of its document pairs differ by a nearly constant 2.4 and 3.0 log units (standard deviations 0.41 and 0.13 over 29 and 26 shared molecules), which suggests unit errors that the 3-unit trimming does not remove. Under the document-grouped split of Section~\ref{sec:docsplit} no task exceeds the floor. In either case $f>1$ signals a problem with the split or the floor, not accuracy beyond the measurement limit.

\paragraph{Decontamination.} Removing molecules that appear in MoleculeNet or TDC changes model scores very little: mean test RMSE moves by at most 0.006 pChEMBL units for every model except ECFP+MLP (at most 0.025), and mean $f$ by +0.018 (Table~\ref{tab:leak}, over the 17 tasks with uncleaned runs). The floors move more than the scores, because decontamination removes replicated molecules preferentially (Section~\ref{sec:data}).

\paragraph{Minimum detectable effect.} The median single-test-set MDE for a paired comparison with ECFP+GBM is 0.047, 0.048 and 0.054 in $f$ for ECFP+RF on random, scaffold and temporal splits and 0.048 on the document-grouped split, and about 0.09 for the embedding models, whose errors are less correlated with the baseline (derivation in Appendix~\ref{app:mde}). These values assume independent test molecules and are therefore optimistic; Section~\ref{sec:support} shows that molecules sharing a source document have strongly correlated errors. The ECFP+RF advantage is below the MDE of a single test set and is detectable only when pooled over tasks, while the embedding gaps on random and scaffold splits are two to three times the MDE.
